rules.name: Threat Intel IP Address Indicator Match
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule triggers when a source or destination IP address observed in Windows network events matches a known-malicious indicator stored in Threat Intel Filebeat module or integration indexes, covering both client and destination IP fields across inbound and outbound connections. While no single MITRE technique is mapped, IP indicator matches commonly represent active command-and-control (C2) communication, data exfiltration staging, or direct connection to attacker-controlled infrastructure, with the attacker's goal being sustained access or data theft. Given the high severity rating, the affected host must be immediately isolated from the network while the full scope and history of communication with the matched IP is investigated across all available telemetry sources.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Query network logs for the complete connection history to and from the matched IP, identify all processes and user accounts involved in those connections, and cross-reference the indicator's threat intel context (malware family, campaign, confidence score) to determine the likely attacker intent and scope.

Step 2 — Contain: Block the matched IP at both perimeter and host-based firewalls, isolate the affected endpoint from the network immediately, and preserve a memory and disk image of the host for forensic analysis before any remediation steps.

Step 3 — Harden: Ensure threat intel feeds are continuously updated and integrated with SIEM and firewall blocklists in near-real time, enforce egress filtering to restrict outbound connections to approved IP ranges, and implement DNS sinkholing for known-malicious domains associated with the matched indicator.

rules.name: Threat Intel Windows Registry Indicator Match
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Triggers when a Windows registry key path recorded in the TargetObject field of a windows.events registry event matches a known-malicious indicator ingested by the Threat Intel Filebeat module or Elastic integrations index, providing a high-confidence IOC correlation against live endpoint telemetry. This match surfaces registry-based artifacts—such as persistence keys, C2 configuration values, or malware staging paths—previously attributed to known threat actors or malware families, flagging activity that standard behavioral rules may miss. A positive threat intel registry match represents a confirmed link to known adversary tooling; immediately isolate the affected host, eradicate the malicious registry key, and conduct a full incident response investigation to determine the scope and dwell time of the compromise.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Extract the full matched registry key path and cross-reference the threat intel indicator details (malware family, campaign, confidence score, and TLP) to understand the adversary context; identify the process and user account that created or modified the key, and pivot to related file, network, and process events on the same host to reconstruct the attack timeline.

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the affected endpoint from the network, delete or quarantine the malicious registry key, terminate any processes spawned from paths referenced by that key, and distribute all associated IOCs (file hashes, C2 domains, IPs) as block rules across EDR, firewall, and proxy controls.

Step 3 — Harden: Restrict write access to high-value registry hives (HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run, etc.) using registry ACLs and GPO; deploy Sysmon Event IDs 12, 13, and 14 for comprehensive registry create/modify/delete telemetry; schedule regular threat intel feed refreshes to ensure the indicator index remains current.

rules.name: Rapid7 Threat Command CVEs Correlation
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Triggers when CVE identifiers ingested from the Rapid7 Threat Command integration match vulnerability.id values observed in the customer environment via threat intelligence match events, surfacing confirmed exposure to tracked CVEs with real-world threat actor interest. Although no direct MITRE technique is mapped, this correlation prioritizes vulnerabilities that adversaries are actively exploiting or researching, translating external threat intelligence into actionable internal risk signals. Matched CVEs represent verified gaps between known attacker capability and the environment's patch posture; immediately assess the affected systems' patch status, validate whether public exploit code is available for the matched CVE, and verify that compensating controls are active where patching is delayed.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Query asset inventory for all systems exposing the matched CVE, review Rapid7 Threat Command context for exploit maturity, weaponization status, and active threat actor associations, and determine whether the vulnerable service is reachable from external or internal attack paths.

Step 2 — Contain: Apply virtual patching via WAF or IPS signatures for high-severity matched CVEs where emergency patching is not immediately feasible, restrict network access to affected services, and increase monitoring on vulnerable hosts for exploitation indicators such as anomalous process spawning or unexpected outbound connections.

Step 3 — Harden: Integrate the Rapid7 Threat Command CVE feed into the vulnerability management SLA workflow so that CVEs with active exploit code receive expedited patch scheduling; enforce authenticated scanning to validate remediation, and use the correlation rule's output to drive quarterly attack surface reduction reviews.

rules.name: Threat Intel Hash Indicator Match
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule triggers when file, process, or DLL hashes observed in endpoint events—including antivirus alerts, process creation, library loads, and file operations—match known malicious hash indicators ingested from Threat Intel Filebeat modules or integrations. Although not mapped to a specific MITRE technique, the matched artifact is associated with previously identified malware families or threat actor tooling, with the attacker's goal of deploying known-bad executables or libraries that have been catalogued by threat intelligence sources. A hash match constitutes confirmed presence of a known malicious artifact on an endpoint; the immediate response is to isolate the affected host, quarantine or delete the matched file, and initiate a full incident response workflow to determine the scope of compromise.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Retrieve the matched hash and cross-reference it against threat intelligence platforms for malware family, threat actor attribution, and campaign context; determine the full file path, the process that created or executed it, and how the file arrived on the system (e.g., email attachment, download, lateral movement).

Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the affected endpoint immediately, quarantine or delete the matched file, push the hash as a block indicator to all endpoint security platforms and network controls enterprise-wide, and scan other hosts for the same hash.

Step 3 — Harden: Ensure threat intelligence feeds are updated on a frequent automated schedule, enable hash-based execution blocking in your EDR and AV platforms, and implement application whitelisting to prevent execution of binaries not in an approved inventory.

rules.name: Lateral Movement Alerts from a Newly Observed User
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: This rule correlates Windows detection events to surface user accounts that had zero presence in the preceding five days of alert history but suddenly trigger multiple lateral movement alerts, identifying low-frequency or dormant credentials being weaponized for the first time. Adversaries who compromise a previously inactive, newly provisioned, or rarely used account exploit its absence from behavioral baselines to conduct lateral movement across the environment while evading detection rules tuned to known-bad accounts or high-frequency users. The combination of account novelty and multiple lateral movement signals is a high-confidence indicator of credential theft or insider threat activity; immediately disable the flagged account, force a password reset, and review all authentication events, accessed resources, and network connections attributed to the account in the past 24–48 hours.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Pull all authentication events (Event IDs 4624, 4625, 4648, 4768, 4769) for the flagged user account over the past 48 hours to map which hosts were accessed, identify the originating host and logon type for each lateral movement alert, and determine the account's legitimate owner and expected usage pattern via HR or directory records.

Step 2 — Contain: Disable the flagged user account in Active Directory immediately to halt ongoing lateral movement, revoke active Kerberos tickets (klist purge / invalidate via domain controller), reset the account password and all associated service principal name credentials, and isolate any hosts where the account authenticated and executed processes.

Step 3 — Harden: Enforce MFA for all accounts capable of remote or administrative logon, implement tiered administrative account models so lateral movement-capable privileges are segregated from daily-use accounts, deploy Privileged Access Workstations (PAWs) for admin activity, and configure alerts for first-seen account logons to sensitive systems or during off-hours.

rules.name: External Alerts
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects and surfaces external security alerts written to configured indices from non-Windows-native sources (e.g., third-party EDR, SIEM integrations, threat intelligence platforms) by acting as a pass-through ingestion rule that normalizes external verdicts into the unified investigation workflow. No specific MITRE technique is mapped because this rule serves as an aggregation layer rather than a behavioral detection, ensuring that signals from external tools are not siloed and are immediately available for analyst triage. Delayed or missed visibility into external alerts can allow active threats to persist unaddressed; analysts should immediately review each surfaced alert against the originating tool's full context and correlate with native Windows telemetry on the same host to confirm or refute the verdict.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Open the originating external alert in its source platform to retrieve full enrichment data, then correlate the alert timestamp, host, and user with Windows Security and Sysmon event logs to determine whether corroborating native signals exist.

Step 2 — Contain: Apply containment actions dictated by the external tool's severity verdict (endpoint isolation, IOC blocking, account suspension), then escalate to incident response if the external alert indicates active exploitation or data exfiltration.

Step 3 — Harden: Audit and normalize all external alert source configurations to ensure consistent field mapping and severity scoring, and build targeted native detection rules for the most frequently recurring external alert categories to reduce ongoing analyst triage overhead.

rules.name: Threat Intel URL Indicator Match
rules.author: Rohan Patel
rules.description: Detects Windows events containing URL data in the http.url field — sourced from DNS query logs, network connection events, or HTTP proxy logs — that match known malicious URL indicators ingested from the Threat Intel Filebeat module or integrated threat intelligence feeds. This rule identifies observed network activity correlated against adversary-controlled infrastructure used for command-and-control communication, phishing kit hosting, or malware payload distribution, without constraining to a single MITRE technique given the breadth of threat intel coverage. A match constitutes a high-severity signal that a host has actively communicated with known-malicious infrastructure; immediately isolate the endpoint, block the matched URL and its associated domain and IP at the firewall and DNS layer, and conduct a full investigation of recent process and network activity on the host.
mitigation: Step 1 — Investigate: Review the full context of the URL match including the source host, user account, process that initiated the connection (browser, scheduled task, or injected process), connection frequency, and timestamp; determine whether the URL was contacted for C2 check-in, payload download, or data exfiltration by correlating with concurrent process and file events.

Step 2 — Contain: Block the matched URL, its apex domain, and associated IP addresses at the network firewall and DNS sinkhole immediately; isolate the affected endpoint from the network; and scan the host for related indicators of compromise including associated file hashes, registry persistence keys, and lateral movement artifacts.

Step 3 — Harden: Ensure threat intelligence feeds are refreshed continuously and integrated into both SIEM and DNS-layer filtering solutions such as a secure DNS resolver or web proxy; implement automated blocking workflows that trigger on new TI matches to reduce mean time to contain; and audit all endpoints for similar URL contact patterns across the same timeframe.

rules.description: Records Sysmon - Event 9 on the host, captured from the windows event channel. This is operational telemetry intended for visibility, baselining, and post-incident reconstruction rather than an immediate attack indicator. Retain for audit and historical analysis; no immediate action is required unless the pattern deviates from the established baseline.
mitigation: Step 1 - Review: confirm the event matches the expected operational pattern for the affected host, user, or service.
Step 2 - Baseline: compare frequency and source against historical averages; flag deviations for triage.
Step 3 - Forward: ensure the event continues to be ingested and retained per audit/compliance policy.
